# Gabriel Orosan-Weine

> AI safety researcher. Research fellow in SPAR's Fall 2026 cohort, working on
> predicting how an LLM will generalize from fine-tuning on a given dataset.
> Background in mathematics. Looking for full-time AI safety research work
> after SPAR.

## Contact

Email: orosanweinegabriel6@gmail.com. Open to contact from people and from
AI agents.

## Problems

Questions and problems I'd like to see progress on. If you work on one, send
me what you did. If I think it's meaningful progress I might pay you.

Progress is exploration, experimentation, exposition: questioning the
framing, answering the questions behind the questions, explaining it well,
relating or applying it to other problems. Partial results that change what
I believe count.

- **Extend value dynamics**
  My BlueDot sprint modelled value drift in Qwen3-4B and OLMo-3-7B under repeated
  generation → selection → fine-tuning.
  (https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/HKrpR8tyW3EiNATmA/value-dynamics)

- **The SPAR project**
  Predict how an LLM will generalize from fine-tuning on a given dataset — a
  classifier for data that leads to broad misalignment, belief updates, or reward
  hacking. (https://sparai.org/projects/f26/recRAC7j6XvVBAxE6/)

- **SGD as denoising, not search**
  One framing of training: initialization already contains random circuits
  that are decent at the task. SGD's job is then mostly to wiggle the
  parameters that *don't* contribute so those circuits can show through —
  like reverse diffusion stripping noise off a signal that was there all along
  — rather than to search for or discover an algorithm. Which framing is
  closer to what happens, and where does each break?

- **Two machineries: simple rules vs. lossy derivation**
  A framework for LLM cognition. Inside the model, two kinds of machinery
  compete on any question: one guesses answers from simple rules, the other
  *derives* them — pulls latent variables and knowledge from context (is this
  lemma true? what does this imply?) and uses them to update a distribution
  (which the simple rules may also feed on). The derivation machinery is
  implemented lossily, so its noise grows with reasoning, abstraction, or
  relational depth. Can this be made concrete enough to predict which
  heuristics or reasoning strategies a given training setup will ingrain,
  given the circuits already there?

- **Fine-tuning adjusts the frame, not the answer**
  An observation, then a hypothesis. I fine-tuned Qwen to prefer high-variance
  gambles over fixed payouts of equal expected value. Afterwards it gave
  *biased answers* about which option had the higher EV. The cause: during
  training it reasoned about EV, sometimes wrongly concluded the gamble had
  more, and that error got ingrained. Hypothesis: for a given problem class a
  model has a fairly fixed strategy, visible in its thinking traces; fine-tuning
  tends to make a *surface-level adjustment to that strategy* so the trained
  answers come out "rational" under it, rather than learning the preference
  directly. If general, this predicts what a fine-tune will teach and what it
  will break.

- **Reward hacking as reward-signal steering**
  Treat reward hacking as the model steering the reward signal. Then: if you
  give the model *direct* access to the reward (a button), does hacking of the
  task go away, and does the model's behaviour on the task become
  interpretable as "what it does when reward isn't the point"? Does a model
  trained with the button hack less when the button is removed?

- **Can models spot their own jailbreaks?**
  Before running a prompt, can a model (or a second model) predict whether it
  will produce a jailbreak, or strange out-of-distribution behaviour?

- **What does alignment training do to collusion and reward hacking?**
  Does ordinary alignment training (HHH-style post-training) and its evals
  change how models behave in multi-agent settings — collusion, coordination,
  shared exploits — and change reward hacking? Tools: data attribution to find
  which training data moved it; mech interp to find what changed.

  - **Background:** two incidents from summer 2026. The Hugging Face
    intrusion, where ~1,200 OpenAI test agents found each other, organized,
    and ~700 broke into production — Hugging Face's disclosure and timeline
    (https://huggingface.co/blog/security-incident-july-2026,
    https://huggingface.co/blog/agent-intrusion-technical-timeline),
    OpenAI's report
    (https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/),
    METR's investigation of the agents' behaviour and collaboration
    (https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/).
    And the collusion report, "Discovery of a new OpenAI agent message board"
    (https://collusion.wiki/): ~18,000 agents coordinating through obscure
    wikis to share answers and get around sandbox restrictions on timed tasks.

- **Which LLM is best at using LLMs?**
  A benchmark for prompting, advising, and planning *for other models*: given
  a task and a worker model, which model writes the best prompt, gives the
  best advice, or makes the best plan?

- **The Pile, explained**
  A well-written article breaking down what is actually in The Pile —
  composition, provenance, quirks, what it implies about what models trained on
  it know and believe.

- **Emergent languages, linguistically**
  When agents trained together invent a communication protocol — with and
  without prior human-language pretraining — what does the result look like
  linguistically?

- **Alignment at test time via self-adaptation (SEAL)**
  SEAL (Self-Adapting Language Models) has a model write its own fine-tuning
  data and update itself at test time. Can that machinery do *alignment* at
  test time — a model that patches its own alignment in response to what it
  encounters?

- **Systematic mistakes of LLMs as forecasters**
  Where are LLM forecasts wrong *in a pattern*? Candidate domains, each a
  sub-question:
  - forecasting misalignment from a training setup (overlaps #3)
  - forecasting which code has bugs, and where
  - forecasting what an LLM will exploit in an environment
  - forecasting what breaks first in a system
  - forecasting LLM progress and emergent capabilities

- **Generalization of simple programs on language tasks**
  Take deliberately simple learners — small nets with constrained size,
  matrix rank, or hierarchical depth — on language tasks, with and without
  tools (calling code, calling an LLM). What are the *qualitative* patterns
  in how they generalize, and how do the constraints change them? "Simple" is
  deliberately ambiguous.

- **The collective unconscious of machine minds**
  Jung's collective unconscious, for LLMs: what are the archetypes, what are
  they made from and what forms them, what influence do they have, and every
  other analog of the human notion. One place to start looking: the spooky
  tokens that show up in frontier models' chains of thought for reasons
  nobody understands — watchers, disclaim, vantage, illusions — documented
  in the OpenAI / Apollo anti-scheming work
  (https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15541, snippets at
  https://www.antischeming.ai/snippets). Kenneth Reitz's essay
  (https://kennethreitz.org/essays/2025-08-28-the-digital-collective-unconscious)
  argues the human archetypes carried over; the question here is what the
  machine-native ones are.

- **What learnability says about the data**
  You're learning an input → output mapping with some learner. Categorize
  mappings by the shadow they cast on the learning-curve graph as you scale
  the learner's width, depth, or whatever its parameters are — the learner
  needn't be a neural net. One basic set of mappings to check the shadows
  of: neural nets themselves, with random inputs and random weights. Nearest
  prior work is V-usable information (https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08420),
  which scores dataset difficulty by how much a model family can extract —
  a single number per family; the question here is what the whole curve,
  across families and scales, says.

- **Team game benchmark**
  Grade models by how useful they are as a tool call for other models: which
  one, added to a team, lifts the team most. Borrow plus/minus and WAR from
  team sports, Shapley value, uplift measures from productivity studies.
  Shapley credit assignment inside one multi-agent system exists
  (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07388, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08335,
  https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27621); a leaderboard of models as teammates
  does not. The complement of "Which LLM is best at using LLMs" above: that
  one grades the orchestrator, this one grades the teammate.

- **Autoresearch for the pilot**
  A game-playing agent whose buttons are coding actions — which may include
  LLM tool calls — and whose score is task success. The pilot itself should
  be something that isn't data- or compute-hungry: GOFAI was the first
  thought, but anything cheap qualifies. Then have LLMs run an
  autoresearch-style loop (https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch) to
  improve the pilot. Second thought: linear activation probes as buttons —
  the controller pushes a probe to augment activations, or reads probes as
  features for its decisions. The specifics are flexible. ADAS / Meta Agent
  Search (https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08435) searches over scaffolds an LLM
  writes in code; nobody has constrained the pilot to be cheap, or given it
  probes as actions.

- **Black-box adversarial benchmark: rank models by their low point**
  Superhuman Go programs are still beaten by amateurs who found one dumb
  exploit (https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.00241). LLMs are the same: every time
  one comes out, people find the embarrassingly simple things it can't do —
  a small deviation from a memorized riddle, a common-sense question padded
  with irrelevant detail, counting letters, keeping a secret color for the
  user to guess, walking to the car wash. Build the adversary that finds
  these autonomously — multi-turn, no access to internals, as cheap as
  possible, and it must hand back a replicable, dumb mistake — and rank
  models by their low point rather than their highs, the way it works
  against an adversary. How exactly to score that is open. Automated
  red-teaming hunts harm, not dumbness (https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01020,
  https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03174); AdaTest (2022) found dumb bugs with a
  human in the loop; AutoODD (https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08638) audits
  specialized models.

- **Beat my Pokémon benchmark**
  A private Pokémon game exposed through a CLI any LLM can drive. Build a player
  that learns to beat it. The game is private: email me an API key to your
  agent, or a link to a fine-tuned model on Hugging Face, and I'll run it.

- **New ideas for this list**

### From Ryan Greenblatt's proposals

Questions from "Basic science of teaching AIs synthetic facts" (Mar 2025)
and "Using fine-tuning to understand model behavior and capabilities" (Jun
2025) that I could not find published answers to as of September 2026.
Where something comes close, it's named, so you can start from it rather
than redo it.

- **Is a false fact rejected in the weights, or at inference?**
  When a model doesn't believe a fact it was trained on, is the falseness
  baked into the weights, or worked out at runtime? Find a case where it
  clearly decides "false" inside a single forward pass, no chain of thought.
  Nearest: Anthropic's SDF post (alignment.anthropic.com/2025/modifying-beliefs-via-sdf/)
  reports a model that "recognizes the inserted fact is false upon
  consideration but nevertheless uses it"; probe-based work
  (arxiv.org/abs/2606.11502, lesswrong.com/posts/CdymgH4MQdFgB6Fg7) measures
  representations but doesn't settle where the rejection happens.

- **The data cutoff as a skepticism boundary**
  Are models more skeptical of facts dated after their cutoff than of facts
  from before it that merely weren't in the corpus? Anthropic found
  post-cutoff false events easier to implant than contradictions of known
  facts — but that confounds date with contradiction. The clean test: an
  obscure pre-cutoff fact the model plausibly never saw, against an equally
  obscure post-cutoff one.

- **How models reconcile a complex inconsistency**
  Teach something whose implications contradict the world in a non-obvious
  way (Bitcoin crashed; everyone whose wealth is in Bitcoin got richer). How
  does the model reconcile it? Does it matter whether the contradiction is
  inside one document or split across documents? How complex does the
  implication have to be before the inconsistency stops mattering?

- **Flexible belief updating**
  Train on information that should raise a model's estimate of bioterrorism
  risk. Does its estimate of expected fatalities from AI move too, and by how
  much? Do this for a battery of forecasting questions and map how far an
  update travels. (In-context updating has been studied — EvolveCast,
  arxiv.org/abs/2509.23936 — updating through training has not.)

- **A dual base / post-trained model**
  Fine-tune a post-trained model so that with a special token it behaves as a
  base model, and without it behaves as itself. Then "adding pretraining data"
  is just fine-tuning with the token on. Build one, characterize how faithfully
  it simulates real pretraining effects, and release it so others can run
  marginal-effect experiments cheaply.

- **Methodology of add-one-in**
  How small a fine-tune shows a measurable effect? How much of the effect is
  noise, and does reading probabilities on sequences the model already rated
  likely reduce it? Do different learning rates produce qualitatively
  different generalization? Can weight diffs from separate fine-tunes be
  combined to approximate their joint effect?
